title: Grouped Histograms and Distribution Shape — Year 9

header.title: Grouped Histograms and Distribution Shape
header.subtitle: Group big data sets, read the shape, and know where the mean sits

meta.lesson-focus: Construct and interpret grouped histograms — age-grouped health data such as lung cancer, leukaemia, stroke; describe distribution shape and explain its connection to the relative positions of mean and median; explore Closing the Gap report data.
meta.ac9-descriptor-text: represent the distribution of multiple data sets for numerical variables using comparative representations; compare data distributions with consideration of centre, spread and shape, and the effect of outliers on these measures
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: Different representations of data distributions can be used to compare features such as centre, shape and spread

html.section0_intro: Last lesson you compared two data sets with parallel dot plots and back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots. Today the data sets get big, so we group them. Warm up your median, mean and skew skills first.
html.section_warmup:
A real health question that is secretly today's statistics.

A hospital is planning its budget for next year: how many stroke-care beds, which rehabilitation services, and for whom. A health manager claims: “Stroke is mainly a problem for older people.”

Two hundred patients are far too many to plot as dots. So the ages are grouped into class intervals (0–9, 10–19, …) and each group becomes one bar of a histogram. The bars touch because age is continuous.

Read the shape: the bars climb to a peak at 70–79 and a thin tail stretches left towards the young patients. That is negative skew.

The shape also tells us something we can't see directly: the few young patients drag the mean age down, so the mean sits below the median. By the end of today you'll be able to use a histogram like this to justify, verify or invalidate a claim, and to say which way the mean and median sit.
html.vocab_cards:
Class interval
Tap to flip
A group of values that data is sorted into, all the same width.
Ages 60–69 is one class interval of width 10.
Frequency
Tap to flip
How many data values fall inside a class interval.
41 stroke patients were aged 60–69.
Grouped histogram
Tap to flip
A graph of grouped numerical data where each class is a bar and the bars touch.
Age groups along the bottom, frequency up the side.
Modal class
Tap to flip
The class interval with the highest frequency: the tallest bar.
For stroke patients the modal class is 70–79.
Positive / negative skew
Tap to flip
Named after the tail: a tail to the right is positive skew, a tail to the left is negative skew.
Incomes: positive skew. Stroke ages: negative skew.
Mean vs median
Tap to flip
The mean is pulled towards the tail; the median barely moves.
Positive skew: mean > median. Negative skew: mean < median.
html.section3_heading: Where does the mean sit? Sort the situations
html.section3_desc: Each situation describes a distribution. Drag it to where its mean would sit compared with its median. Picture the histogram first: where is the tail?
html.sort_activity:
Sort each situation by where the mean sits
Weekly incomes of Australian workers: most earn moderate amounts, a few earn very high amountsAge when people have a stroke: most patients are older, a few are youngHeights of adult men: bunched in the middle, tapering off evenly both waysCars per household: most own 1 or 2, a few own 5 or moreScores on a very easy test: most near full marks, a few very lowMasses of 1 kg bags of flour from a factory: a few grams over or underHouse sale prices in a suburb: most mid-range, a few mansions sell for millionsAge at death in Australia: most people live past 70, a few die young

Mean > median (tail right)

Mean ≈ median (symmetric)

Mean < median (tail left)

💡 The mean uses every value, so a few extreme values in the tail drag it towards the tail. The median is just the middle value, so it hardly moves. That's why the mean sits on the tail side of the median.
html.section4_heading: Match each histogram to its shape
html.worked_example:
A hospital recorded the ages of 24 patients diagnosed with leukaemia (illustrative data). Build a grouped histogram, then describe the shape and test the claim “leukaemia only affects older people”.

3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 15, 28, 35, 44, 52, 58, 61, 63, 66, 67, 69, 71, 72, 74, 76, 78, 81, 85
1
Choose class intervals and count
The ages run from 3 to 85, so classes of width 10 starting at 0 give 9 classes: enough to show the shape, not so many that most are empty. Each value goes in exactly one class: 69 goes in 60–69, 71 in 70–79.
AgeFrequency
0–95
10–192
20–291
30–391
40–491
50–592
60–695
70–795
80–892
Total24
Check: the frequencies add to 24, the number of patients. ✓
2
Draw the histogram
Age groups along the horizontal axis, frequency up the vertical axis, one bar per class, no gaps between bars, title and axis labels.
3
Describe the shape and test the claim
Look for peaks and tails, then connect the shape to the mean and median.
Two peaks, at 0–9 and at 60–79: the distribution is bi-modal.
Median = average of the 12th and 13th ages = (58 + 61) ÷ 2 = 59.5.
Mean = 1133 ÷ 24 ≈ 47.2. The cluster of young children drags the mean well below the median.
ClaimInvalidated: 7 of the 24 patients (29%) were under 20, and the 0–9 class is one of the two tallest bars. Leukaemia mostly affects older adults and young children.

html.we_do_intro:
Read this histogram with the person next to you, then we'll fill in each box as a class. Claim to test: “Most lung cancer patients are aged 60 or over.”

html.strategy_section:
10aSpot the mistake

Jordan grouped the ages of 15 stroke patients into a frequency table before drawing a histogram. Click the line where the mistake first appears.

Ages: 45, 50, 52, 58, 60, 60, 63, 67, 69, 70, 72, 75, 78, 81, 86
Classes: 40–49, 50–59, 60–69, 70–79, 80–89
140–49: frequency 1  (45)
250–59: frequency 4  (50, 52, 58, 60)
360–69: frequency 4  (60, 63, 67, 69)
470–79: frequency 4  (70, 72, 75, 78)
580–89: frequency 2  (81, 86)

✓ Right: that's where the mistake first appears.

Why: 60 is not in the 50–59 class. Each value belongs to exactly one class, and 60 is the first value of 60–69. Jordan counted one of the 60s in the wrong bar. Line 3 is wrong as a knock-on effect: both 60s belong there, giving 5.

Type the correct frequency for the 50–59 class:

10bHinge check🎯 Pick one

A grouped histogram of house sale prices in a suburb has its tallest bars at the low end and a long tail stretching to the right. The median price is $650 000. Which value is most likely the mean?

Long tail to the right  ⟶  mean = ?
Not quite: you moved the mean towards the peak. The tallest bars are where most houses are, but the mean is dragged towards the tail. A few very expensive houses pull the mean up, above the median.
Only if the distribution were symmetric. Mean and median are about equal when both sides balance. Here a long right tail pulls the mean higher than the median.
Correct. Positive skew: a few very expensive houses in the right tail drag the mean up, so the mean is greater than the median of $650 000.
The shape alone tells you the direction. You can't find the exact mean, but a long right tail always pulls the mean above the median. Only one option is above $650 000.

retrieval.hint: Order first: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10. With six values, average the 3rd and 4th.

fb.5: That is the 3rd value only. With an even number of values, average the two middle ones.

retrieval.hint: Add them up, then divide by how many values there are.

retrieval.q: A dot plot has most dots on the left and a long tail stretching to the right. Is it positive or negative skew? Type one word.
retrieval.hint: Skew is named after the direction of the tail. Right is the positive direction on a number line.

fb.negative: Skew is named after the tail, not the peak. The tail points right, towards the higher values.

weDo.q: How many patients are shown in the histogram altogether?
weDo.hint: Add the frequencies on top of the bars: 2 + 6 + 14 + 24 + 30 + 14.

weDo.q: What is the modal class? Type it like 40-49.
weDo.hint: The modal class is the tallest bar.

fb.30: That is the frequency of the tallest bar. The modal class is the age interval underneath it.

weDo.q: How many patients are aged 60 or over?
There are 90 patients, so the median is between the 45th and 46th ages. Which class contains the median? Type it like 40-49.
weDo.hint: Keep a running total from the left: 2, 8, 22, 46, … Which bar takes you past 45?

fb.70-79: That is the modal class (tallest bar). Use a running total of frequencies to find where the 45th age falls.

weDo.q: The tail stretches towards the younger ages. Which is larger: the mean or the median? Type one word.
weDo.hint: A tail to the left drags the mean down towards the young patients.

fb.mean: The mean is pulled towards the tail. This tail points left, to the lower ages, so the mean is the smaller one.

checkpoint.q: What is the shape of this distribution? Type the shape: positive, negative or symmetric.
checkpoint.hint: Find the tallest bars, then look at which way the long, thin tail stretches.

fb.negative: Skew is named after the tail. The thin tail here stretches right, towards the higher earnings.

checkpoint.q: For the earnings histogram above, Which is larger: the mean or the median? Type one word.
checkpoint.hint: The few students earning $400 to $600 are in the tail. Which measure do they drag?

fb.median: The median hardly moves; the mean is dragged towards the tail of high earners.

practice1.q: For the commute-time histogram in P5, Which is larger: the mean or the median? Type one word.

practice1.q: The mean height of the 60 women in P9 is 167.5 cm. The distribution is symmetric. Estimate the median height in cm.
practice1.hint: In a symmetric distribution the mean and median are about the same.

practice2.q: For the screen-time table in S1, the median is between the 10th and 11th values. Type the lower boundary of the class that contains the median.
practice2.hint: Running total: 2, 7, 15, … Which class takes you past 10?

practice2.q: Claim: “More than half of stroke patients are aged 70 or over.” What percentage of these 200 patients were aged 70 or over?
practice2.hint: Add the 70–79 and 80–89 bars, then divide by 200 and multiply by 100.

practice2.q: A grouped histogram of house prices has positive skew and a median of $640 000. The mean is one of $590 000 or $710 000. Type the mean.
practice2.hint: Positive skew: the tail of expensive houses pulls the mean above the median.

fb.590000: That would put the mean below the median, which happens with negative skew. Here the tail points right.

practice2.q: Population A in S5 has a long tail towards the older ages. For population A, Which is larger: the mean or the median? Type one word.

Nine staff at a small business earn a mean salary of $60 000. The owner, who earns $300 000, is added to the data. What is the new mean salary in dollars?

exitProbs.q: A grouped histogram has a long tail stretching to the left. Which is larger: the mean or the median? Type one word.
